title: Sequence alignment: lining up genes across species
interaction: Pick two real protein sequences, such as human and mouse haemoglobin or human and yeast cytochrome c, and fill the dynamic-programming grid cell by cell: each cell takes the best of a match, a gap in one sequence or a gap in the other, and the traceback lights up the optimal alignment. Change the gap penalty or swap BLOSUM62 for an identity matrix and the best alignment shifts; switch from global (Needleman-Wunsch) to local (Smith-Waterman) and only the conserved core survives. Shuffle one sequence a hundred times and the page plots the shuffled scores against the real one.
takeaway: The best alignment of two sequences is found exactly by building it from the best alignments of their prefixes, and a real relative scores far above what shuffled sequences reach.
needs: A handful of protein sequences from UniProt (CC BY 4.0), and the BLOSUM62 substitution matrix (Henikoff & Henikoff 1992, PNAS 89:10915). The matrix is a table of numerical values, freely redistributed in the NCBI BLAST distribution and in Biopython (BSD licence). Cite the paper.
pitfall: An alignment is not proof of shared ancestry: any two sequences have an optimal alignment, and it changes with the scoring matrix and gap penalties; only a score far above the shuffled-sequence background is evidence of homology.
why: MIT 6.047 Computational Biology notes open with global and local alignment by dynamic programming (Needleman-Wunsch, Smith-Waterman): https://ocw.mit.edu/ans7870/6/6.047/f15/MIT6_047F15_Compiled.pdf
overlapWith: dna-to-protein translates one gene; this page compares two genes, and its model is the dynamic-programming alignment and its score statistics, which no existing or proposed page covers (dna-fingerprinting matches repeat lengths, not sequences).
needsSource: UniProt sequences (CC BY 4.0); BLOSUM62, a published numerical table freely redistributed with NCBI BLAST and Biopython (BSD); openly usable with citation

title: Queues: why a nearly busy server is so slow
interaction: Packets (or customers) arrive at random at a router with one output link; set the arrival rate and the service rate and watch the queue grow and drain while a live plot tracks the average wait against the load. Push the utilisation from 50% to 90% to 99% and the wait curve climbs toward a wall, matching Little's law and the M/M/1 formula drawn over the simulated points; make the arrivals or the packet sizes more regular and the same load queues much less.
takeaway: Waiting time stays small until a server is nearly fully busy and then grows without bound, and randomness in the arrivals makes the queue long even when capacity exceeds demand on average.
pitfall: A link that is busy 90% of the time is not 'with 10% to spare': the mean delay at 90% load is about five times that at 50%, and at 99% it is fifty times; average capacity above average demand does not mean no queue.
why: MIT 6.263J Data Communication Networks devotes its core sessions to Little's theorem and the M/M/1 queue: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/electrical-engineering-and-computer-science/6-263j-data-communication-networks-fall-2002/calendar
overlapWith: tcp-congestion-control (proposed) shows senders reacting to a full bottleneck buffer; this page is the queue itself: random arrivals, Little's law and the delay-versus-load curve, with no feedback from the sender.

title: How rivers carve mountains: landscape evolution
interaction: Lift a block of land at a steady rate on a grid and let rain run downhill: each cell drains to its steepest neighbour, rivers erode at a rate set by their drainage area and slope (the stream-power law), and hillslopes creep by diffusion. Watch a branching drainage network and ridges emerge until erosion balances uplift; double the uplift rate and the steady-state mountains grow taller and steeper, make the rock harder and the same happens, then switch the uplift off and watch the relief decay.
takeaway: Mountain ranges reach a steady state in which rivers erode them as fast as tectonics lifts them, so how high and steep they stand is set by the uplift rate and the rock, not by their age.
needs: Optional: a real digital elevation model tile for comparison, from SRTM (NASA/USGS, public domain). The simulation itself needs no data.
pitfall: The stream-power law is an empirical erosion rule with poorly constrained exponents, not a fundamental law; and steady-state topography means the form persists while rock keeps moving up and being removed, not that nothing happens.
why: Landscape evolution modelling with the stream-power incision model (FastScape) is taught as a core geomorphology method, e.g. the Cologne IRTG course by Jean Braun: https://sfb1211.uni-koeln.de/index.php/74-irtg/events/past-events/141-irtg-rtd-landscape-evolution-modeling-using-the-fastscape-algorithm-software
overlapWith: plate-tectonics builds mountains where plates meet; this page adds the erosion that wears them down and shows the drainage network and steady-state relief that emerge from uplift against river incision.

title: Cyclic voltammetry: reading a reaction from a current
interaction: Sweep an electrode's potential up and back down and watch the concentration profile of the oxidised and reduced species near the electrode, solved as diffusion on a 1D grid with Butler-Volmer kinetics at the surface, while the current traces the duck-shaped voltammogram. Speed up the scan and the peaks grow with the square root of the scan rate; slow the electron transfer and the two peaks pull apart from about 57 mV toward an irreversible wave; add a follow-up chemical reaction and the return peak shrinks.
takeaway: The current peaks not when the reaction is fastest but when diffusion can no longer bring fresh molecules to the depleted electrode, and the shape and spacing of the peaks reveal how fast electrons transfer.
pitfall: The peak potential is not the standard potential, and the peak separation of about 57/n mV (2.22RT/nF, often misquoted as 59 mV) holds only for a fast, reversible couple at 25 °C; the current falls after the peak because the diffusion layer thickens, not because the bulk solution has run out.
why: Elgrishi et al., 'A Practical Beginner's Guide to Cyclic Voltammetry', J. Chem. Educ. 2018, 95, 197-206, a widely used teaching reference on how scan rate and electron-transfer kinetics shape a voltammogram: https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.jchemed.7b00361
overlapWith: redox-batteries shows a cell charging and discharging at equilibrium voltages; this page is the measurement technique of electrochemistry, with electrode kinetics and diffusion producing a voltammogram, which nothing on the site models.

title: Switching power supplies: how a charger changes voltage
interaction: Flip a transistor on and off thousands of times a second in a buck converter and watch the inductor current ramp up and down while the capacitor smooths the output; drag the duty cycle and the output settles at that fraction of the input voltage. Compare against a linear regulator dropping the same voltage across a resistor and see the heat meters diverge; lower the switching frequency or shrink the inductor and the ripple grows until the current hits zero, then rearrange the same parts into a boost converter that steps voltage up.
takeaway: A switching converter changes voltage by chopping it and averaging it with an inductor and a capacitor, so it stores and releases energy rather than burning the excess as heat, and output current can exceed input current.
pitfall: A buck converter is not a resistor that drops voltage: ideally it loses no energy, so stepping 20 V down to 5 V draws about a quarter of the output current from the source.
why: MIT 6.334 Power Electronics covers the modelling, analysis and control of DC-DC converters, inverters and rectifiers: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-334-power-electronics-spring-2007/pages/syllabus/
overlapWith: power-grid uses transformers to change AC voltage; this page is the DC-DC switching converter (in every phone charger, laptop and solar inverter), modelled as a piecewise-linear circuit ODE, which no page shows.

title: Drug receptors: dose-response, agonists & antagonists
interaction: Add a drug to a dish of cells and watch it bind receptors by mass action while a log dose-response curve builds point by point; set the drug's affinity and efficacy separately and see potency move the curve sideways while efficacy sets its height. Add a competitive antagonist and the curve slides right in parallel by the Schild ratio, add a non-competitive one and the maximum drops; remove most receptors and a full agonist still gives a full response until its spare receptors run out, while a partial agonist starts blocking the full one.
takeaway: How strongly a drug binds and how strongly it activates are separate properties: a competitive blocker slides the dose-response curve sideways, while a non-competitive one lowers its ceiling once the tissue's spare receptors are used up.
needs: Optional: affinities of a few real agonists and antagonists (e.g. at the beta-adrenergic or mu-opioid receptor) from the IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology (database under the Open Database License, ODbL; text content CC BY-SA 4.0). The model itself (operational model, Gaddum-Schild) needs no data.
pitfall: Potency is not efficacy: a more potent drug is not a stronger one, and a maximal response does not mean every receptor is occupied, since many tissues have spare receptors.
why: MIT OCW HST.151 Principles of Pharmacology, lecture 1 'Drug-Receptor Interactions' (mass action, full and partial agonists, reversible and irreversible antagonists): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/hst-151-principles-of-pharmacology-spring-2005/pages/lecture-notes/
overlapWith: pharmacokinetics-dosing (proposed) follows how the body moves a drug's concentration over time; this page is pharmacodynamics, what that concentration does at the receptor, with agonism, antagonism and spare receptors.
needsSource: none required; optional IUPHAR/BPS Guide to Pharmacology data, ODbL (database) / CC BY-SA 4.0 (text)

title: Where rain comes from: the water cycle
interaction: A side view of sea, land, hills and sky holds a few thousand water parcels. The reader moves one slider, the sunshine, and watches parcels leave the warm sea as vapour, rise, turn into cloud as they cool over the hills, fall as rain and run back down rivers to the sea. Counters show how much water is in the sea, the air, the clouds and the rivers at each moment.
takeaway: The same water goes round and round: the Sun lifts it from the sea, cooling turns it into cloud and rain, and rivers carry it back, so the total never changes.
needs: none (a parcel model with evaporation rising with temperature and condensation when air cools with height; no external data)
pitfall: Clouds are not water vapour: vapour is invisible, and clouds are tiny liquid drops or ice. And evaporation does not need boiling; puddles dry at everyday temperatures, just faster when it is warm.
why: KS2 Year 4 statutory: identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and link the rate of evaporation to temperature (https://thenational.academy/teachers/programmes/science-primary-ks2/units/introduction-to-states-of-matter-and-changing-states/lessons/evaporation-and-condensation-in-the-water-cycle); also NGSS MS-ESS2-4. The catalogue notes the water cycle is not covered.
overlapWith: cloud-base: that page explains why one cloud forms and why its base is flat; this one follows water all the way round the loop, sea to sky to river, and keeps the total constant.

title: How rivers carve valleys
interaction: A sandbox hillside on a grid, like a classroom stream table. The reader tilts it (one control at a time: slope, then how much water) and pours water at the top; the water finds the lowest path, picks up sand where it runs fast and drops it where it slows, cutting a branching valley and building a fan of sand at the bottom.
takeaway: Fast water picks sand up and slow water puts it down, so a steeper slope or more water cuts a deeper valley and builds a bigger fan of sand at the bottom.
needs: none (grid hydraulic-erosion model: water routed downhill, sediment capacity rising with flow speed, erosion and deposition; no external data)
pitfall: Rivers do not dig valleys in one flood or in a single direction downwards; they also drop most of what they carry, and the landscape is as much built by deposition as cut by erosion.
why: NGSS 4-ESS2-1, evidence of weathering and the rate of erosion by water, with slope and water volume as the suggested variables, the classic stream-table investigation (https://thewonderofscience.com/4ess21).
overlapWith: plate-tectonics: that page raises mountains by moving plates; this one wears land down and moves it with running water, which no existing page shows.

title: Why the Moon doesn't fall down
interaction: A cannon stands on a very tall mountain on a round Earth. The reader picks a single thing, how hard to fire, and launches balls one after another; slow ones land close, faster ones land farther around the curve, and one fast enough falls all the way around and comes back to the mountain. A last step swaps the ball for the Moon, far away and moving sideways.
takeaway: Everything thrown falls, but a ball moving sideways fast enough keeps missing the curving ground, so it goes round forever: that is what the Moon and the space station are doing.
needs: none (Newtonian gravity integrated for one body around Earth; Earth radius and surface gravity are standard constants)
pitfall: There is gravity in space: astronauts float because they are falling together with their station, not because gravity has switched off. The Moon is not held up by anything.
why: Newton's cannonball is the standard answer to the child's question why the Moon doesn't fall (https://eg.bucknell.edu/physics/astronomy/astr101/specials/newtscannon.html); KS2 Year 5 requires that unsupported objects fall towards Earth because of gravity, and NGSS 5-PS2-1 that gravity pulls objects down.
overlapWith: orbits-kepler: that page launches bodies around a star to derive ellipses and Kepler's laws with overlays and two planets; this one has one control, starts from throwing a ball, and only reaches the idea that an orbit is falling and missing.

title: Friction: why things slide or stick
interaction: A block sits on a ramp. The reader raises the ramp slowly, one control, and sees the exact angle at which the block starts to slide; then changes the surface (ice, wood, carpet, rubber) or the block's weight and tries again, while an arrow shows the grip of the surface growing to match the pull down the slope until it can't.
takeaway: Friction grips just as hard as it needs to, up to a limit set by the two surfaces, so a heavier block slips at the same angle but ice lets go much sooner than rubber.
needs: Typical static friction coefficients for a few surface pairs from one edition of OpenStax College Physics 2e, Table 5.1 (CC BY 4.0); cite the edition, since rows such as steel on ice differ between versions.
pitfall: Heavier things do not slip later on the same ramp, and for hard surfaces such as wood, metal or ice the size of the touching area hardly matters (soft rubber is the exception); friction is also not only a nuisance, since walking and braking need it.
why: KS2 Year 5 statutory: identify the effects of air resistance, water resistance and friction that act between moving surfaces (https://its.teachit.co.uk/resources/primary/forces-ks2); NGSS 3-PS2-1 balanced and unbalanced forces.
overlapWith: newtons-laws: that page has forces changing motion with carts and projectiles; this one isolates the grip between two surfaces on a tilting ramp, the starting point for kids before any equation.
needsSource: OpenStax College Physics friction table, CC BY 4.0

title: Camouflage: you are the hungry bird
interaction: Moths of many shades rest on a tree trunk and the reader is the bird: tap every moth you spot before the timer runs out. The survivors lay eggs that look like their parents, give or take a little, and the next generation appears; after a few rounds the reader flips the bark from pale to sooty and keeps hunting.
takeaway: The moths you fail to see are the ones that have babies, so after a few generations the moths match the bark, and when the bark changes, so do the moths.
needs: Bark textures, either procedurally generated or public-domain or CC0 photographs from Wikimedia Commons; the moth population model needs no data.
pitfall: A moth does not change colour to hide, and no moth chooses its colour; the population changes because the visible ones are eaten before they breed.
why: England national curriculum, KS2 Year 6 'Evolution and inheritance': identify how animals and plants are adapted to suit their environment and that adaptation may lead to evolution (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-science-programmes-of-study); NGSS MS-LS4-4 (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ls4-4-biological-evolution-unity-and-diversity).
overlapWith: evolution: that page runs a population with sliders for mutation, population size and environment; here the reader is the predator, and the selection is their own clicking, which is the level-0 doorway into that page.
needsSource: none, or CC0/public-domain bark photographs (Wikimedia Commons)

title: Learning by treats: how a robot learns by trying
interaction: A little robot pup sits in a small room with a small biscuit close by, a big bone farther away and a puddle in between. Press play: at first it wanders at random; when it reaches a treat, the tile it stepped from glows warmer, and run after run the warmth spreads back across the floor until the pup walks a glowing path straight to it. One control: how often it tries something new instead of following the warmest tiles. Turn it to zero and the pup keeps settling for the near biscuit; give it some curiosity and it finds the bone.
takeaway: Nobody tells the robot the way; it gets better only because the steps that led to a treat are remembered and tried again, and it needs some random tries to find a better route.
needs: none (tabular Q-learning on a small grid, run live in the browser)
pitfall: The robot does not understand or want the biscuit, and it is not given the map; it only adjusts numbers on tiles. The rewards it is given, not good intentions, decide what it learns, so a badly placed reward teaches the wrong thing.
why: AI4K12 big idea 3, learning, sets grade-band progressions for grades 3-5 and 6-8 (https://www.raspberrypi.org/blog/ai-education-ai4k12-big-ideas-ai-thinking/); reward-trained models (game players, chatbot tuning) are the AI kids already hear about.
overlapWith: reinforcement-learning: that level-2 page exposes value tables, discount factor and learning rate on a paintable grid; this one has one control and a pup-and-treat story, as the level-0 entry to the AI track (and later to rlhf-alignment).

title: Induction heads: how a model copies from its prompt
interaction: Scrub through the training of a tiny two-layer, attention-only transformer (one head per layer) on sequences that repeat partway through, from a fixed-seed run whose checkpoints ship with the page, or retrain it live; watch the loss sit on a plateau and then fall suddenly. At any checkpoint, hover a token in a test sequence to see each head's attention: after the drop, the layer-1 head looks at the previous token and the layer-2 head attends to whatever followed the earlier copy of the current token. Switch off either head and the in-context copying stops.
takeaway: A transformer learns to continue a pattern seen earlier in its prompt with a two-head circuit, one head marking each token's predecessor and another finding the earlier match and copying what followed, and that circuit appears all at once as a sudden drop in the loss.
needs: Checkpoints of a tiny attention-only transformer trained on synthetic repeated-token sequences, produced by the project (or trained live in the browser), following the setup of Olsson et al. 2022 and Singh et al. 2024 (arXiv 2404.07129); no external data.
pitfall: Induction heads do not explain all in-context learning: they copy what is already in the context, and abilities such as learning a new mapping from examples need more than this circuit.
why: Anthropic's 'In-context Learning and Induction Heads' and its follow-ups are a core mechanistic-interpretability result, studied at ICML 2024: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07129
overlapWith: transformers: that page shows the attention weights of a trained model on fixed sentences; this one trains a model live, shows one specific two-head circuit forming during a phase change, and tests it by switching heads off.
needsSource: none (synthetic data, model trained by the project; only the published method is reused)

title: Superposition: more features than neurons
interaction: Train a tiny network in the browser to squeeze five input features through two hidden neurons and rebuild them, and see each feature's direction drawn as an arrow in the 2D hidden space. Slide how rarely each feature is active: with dense features the network keeps two of them at right angles and drops the rest; sparser, it packs four as two pairs of opposite arrows; sparser still, the arrows spread into a pentagon that stores all five, at the cost of some interference. Change the importance of each feature and watch which ones lose their arrows.
takeaway: When features are rarely active at the same time, a network stores more of them than it has dimensions by sharing directions among them and accepting some interference, and the arrangement jumps between distinct shapes (two at right angles, opposite pairs, a pentagon) as sparsity grows.
needs: None: the toy model (ReLU output, tied weights, importance-weighted loss) trains in the browser in seconds, as in Elhage et al. 2022, 'Toy Models of Superposition' (Transformer Circuits).
pitfall: The page must not claim that each neuron in a real LLM stands for one concept, nor that this toy proves exactly how large models store facts; superposition is why single neurons are often hard to interpret.
why: 3Blue1Brown's 'How might LLMs store facts' (Deep Learning chapter 7) ends on the superposition hypothesis: https://3blue1brown.substack.com/p/how-might-llms-store-facts-chapter
overlapWith: embeddings: that page shows the directions of pretrained word vectors; this one trains a network live to show how and when it packs more features than dimensions into one space.
needsSource: none (trained in the browser on synthetic data)

title: Retrieval: how a chatbot looks things up
interaction: Pick one of several questions about a small shelf of documents. Watch the documents split into chunks and embed as points; the question becomes a point too, and the nearest chunks light up and are pasted into the prompt. Change the chunk size and the number of chunks retrieved, or remove the document that holds the answer, and compare a small model's next-token probabilities for the answer with and without the retrieved text (precomputed for every combination).
takeaway: A chatbot that 'searches' does not change its weights: it finds the passages whose embeddings sit closest to the question and puts them into the prompt, so its answer is only as good as what retrieval put there.
needs: A small document set, either public-domain texts (for example NASA or US government pages) or Simple English Wikipedia excerpts (CC BY-SA 4.0); embeddings from all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Apache 2.0), run in the browser or precomputed; next-token probabilities with and without context from a small open model such as SmolLM2-135M-Instruct (Apache 2.0), precomputed.
pitfall: Retrieval does not make answers true: a model can still ignore or misread the retrieved passage, and the nearest chunk by embedding is not always the one that answers the question.
why: Stanford CS224V lists retrieval-augmented generation among its topics (https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224v), and Stanford CS25 recorded a lecture on retrieval-augmented language models (https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs25/recordings).
overlapWith: embeddings: that page measures nearness between word vectors; this one uses nearness between question and passage vectors to choose what goes into a language model's prompt, and shows the effect on its answer.
needsSource: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Apache 2.0); SmolLM2 (Apache 2.0); documents public domain or CC BY-SA 4.0 (share-alike must be honoured)

title: Microwave ovens & their hot spots
interaction: Switch on a microwave oven seen from above: a wave simulation fills the metal box, and a slab of food warms where the field is strong, shown as a heat map. Stop the turntable to see fixed hot and cold spots, start it to even them out, and lay a chocolate bar across the floor to measure the gap between melted spots against the wavelength.
takeaway: Microwaves reflecting off the metal walls form a standing pattern of strong and weak spots that stays fixed in the box, which is why food heats unevenly and why the turntable moves the food through it.
needs: None: a 2D finite-difference wave (or Helmholtz) solver in a rectangular cavity at 2.45 GHz with a lossy dielectric slab; standard permittivity values for water and food from textbook tables.
pitfall: 2.45 GHz is not a special resonance of water molecules, and microwaves do not cook food from the inside out; they heat the outer few centimetres, and the chocolate spacing is only roughly half a free-space wavelength because the cavity's modes are not a simple standing wave.
why: The chocolate-in-the-microwave speed-of-light experiment is a classic school lesson: https://www.bu.edu/gk12/loren/lesson_microwave.html
overlapWith: waves-interference: that page shows standing waves and interference on strings and in open space; this one applies them in a closed metal box with an absorbing load, where the pattern decides what gets hot.

title: Lightning: how a bolt finds the ground
interaction: Charge a thundercloud above a landscape and watch a stepped leader grow down from it in jagged jumps, each step chosen at random but more likely where the electric field is strongest. Add a tree, a tower or a lightning rod: an upward streamer rises to meet the leader, the channel connects and the bright return stroke runs from the ground up. Raise or lower the cloud's charge and compare how often the tall object is the one that gets hit.
takeaway: Lightning branches because it grows step by step toward wherever the electric field is strongest, and tall pointed objects make the field strong enough near them to launch a streamer that often, but not always, catches the leader.
needs: None: the dielectric breakdown model (Niemeyer, Pietronero and Wiesmann 1984), which solves the Laplace equation on a grid and grows the channel with probability proportional to a power of the local field; stroke timings and currents from NOAA/NWS public-domain material.
pitfall: The bright flash does not travel down from the cloud: the visible return stroke goes up the channel from the ground; and lightning can strike the same place twice. The model's branching exponent is fitted, not derived, and a 2D grid gives flatter branching than real 3D bolts.
why: The US National Weather Service explains the stepped leader and return stroke for the public: https://weather.gov/safety/lightning-science-negative-charged-flash
overlapWith: atmosphere-weather: that page covers winds, fronts and storms at the scale of the globe; this one zooms into one discharge and models how its path grows and where it lands.
needsSource: none (computed model; facts from NOAA/NWS, US public domain)

title: Static electricity: why a balloon sticks to the wall
interaction: Rub a balloon on a jumper, one stroke at a time, and count the tiny charges that hop from the jumper to the balloon. Bring the balloon near a wall: the wall's charges lean away or toward it without leaving, and the balloon sticks. Hang two rubbed balloons side by side and they push each other apart.
takeaway: Rubbing moves charges from one thing to another; opposite charges pull and like charges push, and even an uncharged wall is pulled because its charges shift a little toward or away from the balloon.
needs: None: point charges with Coulomb forces; the jumper, balloon and wall are insulators whose charges shift slightly in place, as in PhET's model.
pitfall: Rubbing does not create charge, it only moves it from one thing to the other (the tiny charged bits that move are not the atoms' centres), and the wall the balloon sticks to is not itself charged overall: its charges only shift a little.
why: PhET's 'Balloons and Static Electricity' is one of its most used simulations (CC BY): https://clixplatform.tiss.ac.in/phet/en/simulation/balloons.html
overlapWith: magnets-and-poles: that page is about magnetic poles, which always come in pairs; this one is about electric charges that can be separated and moved by rubbing.
